s50l:S1Q04F.q: How would you reduce the sorting cost for millions of customers while preserving the tie rule?
s50l:S1Q04F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:S1Q04F.spoken: I'd avoid full global sorting by using a min-heap or quickselect to pull top customer rankings in linear time instead of O(N log N). To preserve the tie rule, I tack on the customer ID as a stable secondary key so identical scores always resolve deterministically. If the dataset is massive, I'd use parallel local partition sorting followed by a k-way merge.

s50l:S1Q06F.q: How would you index those tables, and what changes if historical records can be corrected after ingestion?
s50l:S1Q06F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:S1Q06F.spoken: I'd put a composite index on customer ID and timestamp since range queries and timeline filtering drive most of our reads. If historical records get corrected after ingestion, I'd switch to an append-only model with effective-date versioning instead of in-place updates, so we can re-evaluate past states correctly without breaking downstream analytics or model features.

s50l:S2Q05F.q: An example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependencies.
s50l:S2Q05F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:S2Q05F.spoken: Imagine a financial audit query requiring two distinct subsidiary revenue figures buried in separate footnotes; a greedy retriever might grab the same high-level executive summary chunk twice because it matches global keyword density, missing the second subsidiary entirely. To fix coverage gaps, I incorporate redundancy by applying Maximal Marginal Relevance to penalize semantic duplication, ensuring top-k results introduce fresh information rather than repeating adjacent text. For multi-hop dependencies, I use agentic query decomposition where an intermediate reasoning node evaluates the first retrieved chunk to dynamically generate a follow-up sub-query for the remaining evidence.

s50l:S2Q08F.q: How do you prove the replacement index is sufficiently complete and current before you send production traffic to it?
s50l:S2Q08F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:S2Q08F.spoken: I validate a replacement index by running a shadow evaluation pipeline against our golden test set, comparing metrics like multi-hop accuracy and retrieval recall directly against the legacy index. To ensure completeness, I run an automated parity check verifying that the total document count and ID sets match our primary PostgreSQL store. Finally, I confirm currency by checking ingestion stream offsets to guarantee zero lag before shifting traffic over.

s50l:D1.q: How would you index those tables, and what changes if historical records can be corrected after ingestion?
s50l:D1.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:D1.spoken: For indexing, I'd put B-tree indexes on primary and foreign keys along with high-cardinality filter columns, and use partial indexes for active rows to keep overhead low. If historical records can be corrected, in-place updates cause severe index bloat and write amplification. To handle that cleanly, I'd switch to an append-only or temporal table pattern with valid-time ranges, where updates insert new versions rather than overwriting existing data.

s50l:D2.q: An example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependencies.
s50l:D2.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:D2.spoken: If you're looking at a complex vendor contract, a greedy relevance search might pull three chunks that all repeat the main indemnity definition because of high keyword overlap, completely missing the liability cap clause buried in the appendix. To fix coverage gaps, I incorporate redundancy by applying Maximal Marginal Relevance to penalize semantic duplicates and force the retriever to surface diverse sub-sections. For multi-hop dependencies, I use agentic query decomposition—similar to what I implemented at Koolay—where a workflow breaks a complex question into sequential sub-queries, chaining intermediate retrieval steps together before synthesizing the final answer.

s50l:D3.q: How do you prove the replacement index is sufficiently complete and current before you send production traffic to it?
s50l:D3.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50l-A
s50l:D3.spoken: I run an automated validation suite that compares the replacement index against a golden test set of queries, tracking recall and semantic similarity metrics against the active index. To verify currency, I cross-reference record counts and max timestamps against the source PostgreSQL database to confirm zero sync lag. Finally, I run a shadow evaluation period to compare live response distributions before updating the traffic pointer.
